    "acs-selection"="Direct Acs equals TRUE only for an exact parent-agency key in the dynamic ideal-point data. Pairs count witness--member--hearing rows. Administration-specific matches require a separate join.",

agency_note_v2 <- function(codes) {
  d <- dyad_b_raw %>% filter(agencycode %in% codes) %>% distinct(agencycode, opm_agencyname) %>% arrange(agencycode, opm_agencyname)
  z <- vapply(split(d$opm_agencyname, d$agencycode), function(z) paste(tools::toTitleCase(tolower(z)), collapse=", "), character(1))
  z <- gsub("U.s.", "United States", z, fixed = TRUE)
  paste(paste(names(z), "=", z), collapse="; ")
}

# count main-body words (introduction through conclusion) for the title page
count_body_words <- function(path) {
  # read the source and keep the lines from the introduction up to the references
  txt <- readLines(path, warn = FALSE)
  body <- txt[grep("^# Introduction", txt):(grep("^# References", txt) - 1)]
  # drop fenced blocks (r chunks and raw latex figure notes), including the fence lines
  fence <- grepl("^```", body)
  body <- body[!(fence | cumsum(fence) %% 2 == 1)]
  body %>%
    paste(collapse = " ") %>%
    # drop html comments and display equations
    stringr::str_remove_all("<!--.*?-->") %>%
    stringr::str_remove_all("\\\\begin\\{equation\\}.*?\\\\end\\{equation\\}") %>%
    stringr::str_remove_all("\\$\\$.*?\\$\\$") %>%
    stringr::str_replace_all("`r [^`]+`", " x ") %>%
    # count each inline formula, citation bracket, and cross-reference as one word
    stringr::str_replace_all("\\$[^$]+\\$", " x ") %>%
    stringr::str_replace_all("\\[[^\\]]*@[^\\]]*\\]", " cite ") %>%
    stringr::str_replace_all("\\\\@ref\\([^)]*\\)|\\\\ref\\{[^}]*\\}", " 1 ") %>%
    # drop remaining latex commands and section attributes such as {.unnumbered}
    stringr::str_remove_all("\\\\[a-zA-Z]+") %>%
    stringr::str_remove_all("\\{[^}]*\\}") %>%
    # split on white space and keep tokens that contain a letter or digit
    stringr::str_split("\\s+") %>%
    unlist() %>%
    stringr::str_detect("[[:alnum:]]") %>%
    sum()
}

# Abstract {.unnumbered}

\begingroup\abstractstretch Congress relies on bureaucrats for information about how policy works. @ban2026 show that bureaucrats give less analytical information to legislators from the party opposite the president. Yet agencies hold policy views of their own, and some are built to resist presidential control. I argue that agency alignment and agency independence shape both who questions an agency and what its witnesses say. Treating House hearings from 1997 to 2014 as a network of legislators and agencies, I show that a few cabinet departments reach many members. Communities of members partly follow committee jurisdiction and cut across party lines. With continuous measures of agency ideology and independence, I find that the out-partisan gap in legislative hearings grows as an agency's ideology moves closer to the president's. In oversight hearings, the gap is smaller when an agency's decision makers are more independent of the president. These patterns suggest that committees organize who hears from an agency, while agency alignment and independence condition how much analysis its witnesses give.

\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} Agency Ideology, Agency Independence, Bipartite Networks, Congressional Hearings, Information Sharing\par\endgroup

```{r word-count, results='asis'}
# print the computed main-body word count below the keywords
cat("\\par\\noindent\\textbf{Word count:}",
    format(count_body_words(knitr::current_input(dir = TRUE)), big.mark = ","),
    "\\par\n")
```

\newpage

# Introduction {.unnumbered}

Congress depends on the executive branch for information about how policy works. Bureaucrats know how programs run and where they fail [@gailmard2012]. Committee hearings are one of the few public settings where members can question them directly. @ban2026 measure the analytical content of bureaucrats' answers in House hearings from 1997 to 2014. They find that bureaucrats give less analytical information to members from the party opposite the president. The gap is larger for political appointees.

Their design studies what is said once a member and a bureaucrat meet. It does not ask which members question which agencies. That question matters for information sharing. A member who never questions an agency's witnesses receives none of their testimony. If members sort toward agencies that share their views, a gap measured within exchanges describes only part of the flow of information between the branches.

Agencies also differ in ways that the presidential divide can miss. Many hold policy views that persist across Democratic and Republican administrations [@richardson2018]. I use *agency ideology* for an agency's perceived position on a liberal--conservative scale [@clinton2008; @richardson2018]. I use *agency alignment* for the relationship between an agency's ideology and the party of a political actor. A Republican member is aligned with a conservative agency and a Democratic member with a liberal one. The president is aligned with an agency in the same way. @ban2026 test one version of this idea in Table B8 of their appendix. They split agencies at the median of the ideology score of @richardson2018. Out-partisans receive even less analytical information from agencies aligned with the president. A second trait is *agency independence*, the structural protection of an agency from presidential control. Presidents and Congress build this protection into some agencies through fixed terms or exemptions from review [@lewis2003; @selin2015].

I extend this work with the authors' replication data in three ways. First, I treat questioning as a bipartite network of members and agencies. I describe its centrality and closure along with its community structure. Second, I replace the median split with continuous measures of agency alignment and agency independence. Third, I specify a bipartite exponential random graph model (ERGM) to test whether aligned members are more likely to question an agency.

The network analysis focuses on the 113th Congress (2013--2014). It is the most recent Congress in the replication data. It also had divided government. Republicans held the House majority under a Democratic president, so the president's out-partisans chaired the committees that invited agency witnesses. Oversight hearings make up 58 percent of its hearings, the largest share of any Congress in the data. In the replication data, agencies with an ideology score account for 88 percent of its witness--member rows. The survey behind that score took place in 2014, which places the measure closest in time to this Congress [@richardson2018]. Earlier Congresses show similar closure, so the 113th is not an unusual case (Appendix C).

In the 113th Congress, 419 members questioned witnesses from 51 agency codes. Witnesses from the Department of Defense (DD) answered questions from 54 percent of these members. The median member questioned six agencies. Members share agencies far more often than in a random reference that keeps each member's activity fixed. The five communities I find in the member projection mix Democrats and Republicans. Their agreement with party is near zero. Their agreement with each member's most frequent committee is modest but positive. Together these patterns suggest that committees shape the network.

I reproduce the four published tables I use at their reported precision. @ban2026 place agencies without an ideology score in the nonliberal group. When I instead restrict the sample to agencies with a score, the interaction in legislative hearings stays at $-0.62$ with a standard error (SE) of 0.21. The interaction in oversight hearings falls to $-0.29$ (SE 0.24) and is no longer significant at the 5 percent level.

The continuous measures agree with the Table B8 results on the restricted sample. In legislative hearings the out-partisan gap grows as the agency's ideology moves toward the president's. In oversight hearings this pattern is weak, but the gap is smaller in agencies whose decision makers are more independent of the president. An exploratory test suggests that in oversight hearings the gap grows faster with alignment in science agencies. That result reverses when I drop the Environmental Protection Agency (EP). All of these estimates are conditional associations among observed exchanges.

These results add to research on interbranch information in two ways. First, studies of hearings measure what witnesses say once a member asks [@ban2026]. Studies of oversight ask which agencies Congress targets [@clinton2014; @lowande2018]. A network of questioning links the two stages. It first shows which members question each agency. Only then can we ask what the agency tells them. Second, @ban2026 explain the content gap through the witness's tie to the president. Agency ideology and agency independence offer two other links between a witness and the president. Separating them helps identify the mechanism. If ideology drives the gap, the gap reflects goals that witnesses share with the president. If independence narrows the gap, the gap reflects the president's control over who leads the agency.

The next section defines agency ideology and develops four hypotheses about alignment and agency independence. I then describe the data and the questioning network. The following sections reproduce the published estimates and report the extension estimates before laying out the network model. I close with the intergovernmental context of these hearings and the limits of this research.

# Agency Alignment and Information Sharing {.unnumbered}

@ban2026 treat bureaucrats as agents of the president. In their account, a member of the president's party is aligned with the witness and a member of the other party is not. This view fits political appointees well because the president chooses them. Career officials are a harder case. They stay across administrations, and their agencies develop policy commitments that outlast any one president [@clinton2008]. These commitments can place an agency closer to one party than to the president. A Republican member can therefore share the views of a conservative agency under a Democratic president.

## Agency Ideology {.unnumbered}

Agency ideology is an agency's position on the liberal--conservative scale as informed observers perceive it. @clinton2008 treat it as the policy preferences that experts attribute to an agency. @richardson2018 measure it as the perceived policy leanings of an agency across Democratic and Republican administrations. Their survey describes these leanings as arising from law and practice along with culture and tradition. Agency ideology matters because presidents treat ideologically distant agencies as sources of resistance. They place more political appointees in agencies whose views differ from theirs [@lewis2008]. In hearings, ideology may also shape whom a witness treats as an ally. A witness from a liberal agency may see a Democratic member as a supporter of its programs even under a Republican president.

Researchers cannot observe agency ideology directly, so they infer it. @clinton2008 combine expert ratings of agencies in an item response model. @clinton2012 survey federal executives and place agencies on a common scale with presidents and members of Congress. @richardson2018 use the 2014 Survey on the Future of Government Service. It asked federal executives whether the policy views of each agency slant liberal or conservative across administrations. A Bayesian item response model turns these ratings into scores for 165 agencies. Negative scores denote liberal agencies and positive scores conservative ones. @acs2025 instead infers agency ideology from regulatory review. Agencies list their planned rules in the Unified Agenda, and the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) decides which rules to review for the president. An item response model treats review decisions as signals of the distance between the president and the agency. Agency ideal points can shift from one administration to the next. Anchoring presidents at their NOMINATE scores places these ideal points on the same scale as members of Congress.

@ban2026 use the score of @richardson2018. Their Table B8 codes an agency as liberal when its score falls below the median and as nonliberal otherwise. An agency is aligned with the president when this label matches the president's party. The binary code is simple to interpret. But it treats agencies just above and just below the median as different, and it requires a choice about agencies without a score.

I keep the score of @richardson2018 as the primary measure because it covers the most agency codes in the hearing data. Instead of splitting the score at the median, I center it at the median agency and use it as a continuous measure. I then multiply it by the party of the member or the president. This product measures agency alignment and is positive when the two lean the same way. The estimates of @acs2025 vary by administration but match only 11 agency codes, so I use them for robustness checks. A later version will also compare results with the scores of @clinton2008 and @clinton2012.

## Two Stages of Information Sharing {.unnumbered}

Information sharing in hearings has two stages. A member first decides whether to question a witness from a given agency. The witness then decides how much analysis to give. Alignment can matter at both stages.

Members choose whom to question within limits. Committees set the agenda and invite the witnesses. A member can question only agencies that appear before the member's committees. In a policy network, @leifeld2012 find that opportunity structures absorb the effect of shared preferences on information exchange. A test of alignment must therefore condition on opportunity. Within those opportunities, members may still prefer agencies whose work they support. An aligned agency can supply evidence that helps a member defend shared programs.

*Questioning Ties Hypothesis (H1).* Among member--agency pairs with a verified opportunity to meet, a member is more likely to question an agency when the member's party is aligned with the agency's ideology.

Research on oversight gives a reason to expect the opposite. @clinton2014 place agencies and committees on a common scale and relate oversight to their policy differences. In that account, members question distant agencies to pull them toward their own positions. Hostile oversight therefore predicts that misaligned members are more likely to question an agency. The questioning ties hypothesis (H1) and this rival make opposite predictions about the same coefficient. Members also contact agencies outside hearings. In agency correspondence logs, committee roles and district interests matter more than ideological conflict [@lowande2018]. A hearing tie therefore captures only the public part of this contact.

Once a member and a witness meet, the witness chooses how much analysis to give. @ban2026 find less analytical information for presidential out-partisans. Their Table B8 suggests that the gap is larger in agencies aligned with the president. Officials in such agencies are more likely to share the president's goals. They therefore have more reason to treat the president's opponents as critics.

*Analytical Content Hypothesis (H2).* Conditional on an exchange, presidential out-partisans receive less analytical information. The gap is larger when the agency's ideology is closer to the president's.

The analytical content hypothesis (H2) restates the Table B8 expectation with a continuous measure. It compares agencies along the whole range of ideology rather than on two sides of a cutoff.

## Agency Independence {.unnumbered}

Presidents reach agencies through appointments and review. Agency design limits that reach. @lewis2003 shows that presidents and Congress choose design features in part to protect agencies from future political control. @selin2015 measures this protection as structural independence. She codes 50 structural features in the statutes of 321 federal agencies and estimates two dimensions with a Bayesian latent variable model. The first dimension is the independence of decision makers. It reflects limits on appointment and removal such as fixed terms and party-balancing rules. The second is the independence of policy decisions. It reflects limits on political review such as exemption from review by the Office of Management and Budget (OMB). Higher scores denote more independence on each dimension.

Agency independence is separate from agency ideology. An independent agency can still lean liberal or conservative. @hollibaugh2018 show that nominee ideology and agency independence jointly shape presidential nominations and Senate confirmation. If witnesses give less to out-partisans because they answer to the president, the gap should shrink where the president's hold is weaker. Limits on who leads an agency weaken that hold most directly.

*Agency Independence Hypothesis (H3).* The out-partisan gap in analytical information is smaller in agencies with more independent decision makers.

Policy-decision independence is a separate test. It concerns review of what an agency does and not who leads it. Limits on review do not change who directs a witness, so I report its interaction without a directional prediction. I use both scores of @selin2015 as continuous measures. I also describe agencies with the four-level leadership category of @fazekas2023, who follow the agency types of @dahlstrom2021. It separates executive departments from distinct bureaus within them. It also separates independent administrations outside the cabinet from independent commissions. The category is coarser than the Selin scores [@selin2015], so I use it only to describe agencies in Appendix B.

## Scientific Expertise and Rival Expectations {.unnumbered}

Agencies with scientific missions may follow a different pattern. Civil servants who see their agency as politicized are more likely to leave and less likely to build expertise [@richardson2019]. The two parties also differ in how much their policy documents draw on science [@furnas2025]. If partisan conflict over science extends to hearings, science agencies may show a larger gap. I group five agencies as science agencies because their missions rest on scientific research or technical regulation. Two are the Department of Energy (DN) and the Environmental Protection Agency (EP). The other three are the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NN) and the National Science Foundation (NF) along with the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NU).

*Scientific Agencies Hypothesis (H4).* In science agencies, the out-partisan gap grows faster than in other agencies as the agency's ideology moves closer to the president's.

Professional norms point the other way. Scientists and engineers work under norms that reward analysis for any audience, which could narrow the gap in science agencies. The scientific agencies hypothesis (H4) is exploratory because five agencies give little variation. I report all lower-order terms. I also drop each science agency in turn to check whether one agency drives the result.
