```{r replication-variables, eval=TRUE, include=FALSE}
# preserve each stata script's transformations
rep_b <- dyad_b_raw %>% mutate(
  comid = interaction(chamber, cmt_govtrack, drop = TRUE),
  presid = factor(pres), agencyid = factor(agencycode), hid = factor(hearingid),
  polappt2 = as.numeric(polappt_type == "PAS"),
  polappt2 = ifelse(agencycode == "DD", NA_real_, polappt2),
  polappt2 = ifelse(!is.na(dod_pol), dod_pol, polappt2),
  pres_outparty = ifelse(pres_party %in% c(0, 1), 1 - pres_party, NA_real_),
  polappt_presoutparty = polappt2 * pres_outparty,
  mc_extreme = abs(party_median_ideo - dwnom1),
  bureau_dem = as.integer(!is.na(agency_ideo) & agency_ideo < -0.1256831),
  pres_dem = as.integer(pres %in% c("clinton", "obama")),
  pres_align = as.integer(bureau_dem == pres_dem),
  outparty_aligned = pres_outparty * pres_align,
  num_word = log1p(num_word), word_count_ask = log1p(word_count_ask),
  word_count = log1p(word_count))
# table 3 does not log word_count_ask
rep_nonb <- dyad_raw %>% group_by(hearingid) %>%
  mutate(bureauappear = max(bureaucrat)) %>% ungroup() %>%
  filter(bureaucrat != 1) %>% mutate(
    comid = factor(committee_code2), presid = factor(pres),
    hid = factor(hearingid), typeid = factor(type),
    pres_outparty = ifelse(pres_party %in% c(0, 1), 1 - pres_party, NA_real_),
    mc_extreme = abs(party_median_ideo - dwnom1))
rep_aggregate <- aggregate_raw %>% mutate(
  tot_q_b = q_b_co + q_b_out, tot_q_nb = q_nb_co + q_nb_out,
  tot_q = tot_q_b + tot_q_nb, tot_q_co = q_b_co + q_nb_co,
  tot_q_out = q_b_out + q_nb_out,
  tot_a_b = a_b_co + a_b_out, tot_a_nb = a_nb_co + a_nb_out,
  tot_a = tot_a_b + tot_a_nb,
  tot_w_b = log1p(w_b_co + w_b_out),
  tot_w_nb = log1p(w_nb_co + w_nb_out),
  tot_w = log1p(w_b_co + w_b_out + w_nb_co + w_nb_out),
  ln_tot_a = log1p(tot_a))
inst_v2 <- c("pres_outparty", "majority", "chairspeech", "rankmemspeech", "mc_extreme", "les")
committee_v2 <- c("subcommittee", "bill", "numwitness", "dyad_order_h")
question_v2 <- c("gscore_ask", "posi_ask", "nega_ask", "acount_ask", "word_count_ask")
# areg counts absorbed fe in residual degrees of freedom, including nested fe
rep_fit_v2 <- function(data, rhs, fe, outcome = "ascore", cluster = "hid") {
  # keep stata's one absorbed fe; explicit factors retain its collinearity/df convention
  explicit <- paste0("factor(", fe[-1], ")")
  f <- as.formula(paste(outcome, "~", paste(c(rhs, explicit), collapse = " + "), "|", fe[1]))
  fit <- fixest::feols(f, data = data, vcov = as.formula(paste0("~", cluster)),
    fixef.rm = "none", collin.tol = 1e-8,
    ssc = fixest::ssc(K.adj = TRUE, K.fixef = "full", K.exact = TRUE, G.adj = TRUE),
    notes = FALSE, nthreads = 1)
  fit$rep_fe <- fe
  fit
}
# published term labels and stacked clustered standard errors
term_labels_v2 <- c(pres_outparty="President out-partisan", polappt2="Political appointee",
  polappt_presoutparty="President out-partisan x Political appointee", majority="Majority party",
  chairspeech="Committee chair", rankmemspeech="Ranking member", mc_extreme="Ideological extreme",
  les="LES", subcommittee="Subcommittee", bill="Referral hearing", numwitness="Number of witnesses",
  dyad_order_h="Dyad order", gscore_ask="Grandstanding score", posi_ask="Share of positive tone",
  nega_ask="Share of negative tone", acount_ask="Analytical word count",
  word_count_ask="(ln) Number of legislator words", pres_align="President-Aligned",
  outparty_aligned="President out-partisan x President-Aligned", divided_house="Divided government",
  P="Presidential agency alignment", OP="Out-partisan x Alignment",
  OS1="Out-partisan x Decision-maker independence", OS2="Out-partisan x Policy-decision independence",
  OScience="Out-partisan x Science agency", PScience="Alignment x Science agency",
  OPScience="Out-partisan x Alignment x Science agency")
rep_display_v2 <- function(models, terms = NULL, controls = FALSE, kind = "agency", means = NULL) {
  if (is.null(terms)) terms <- unique(unlist(lapply(models, function(m)
    names(coef(m))[!startsWith(names(coef(m)), "factor(")])))
  labels <- unname(term_labels_v2[terms])
  stopifnot(!anyNA(labels))
  out <- data.frame(Term = as.vector(rbind(labels, "")))
  for (j in seq_along(models)) {
    m <- models[[j]]; b <- coef(m)[terms]; se <- fixest::se(m)[terms]
    pv <- fixest::pvalue(m)[terms]
    stars <- ifelse(pv < .001, "***", ifelse(pv < .01, "**", ifelse(pv < .05, "*", "")))
    out[[paste0("(", j, ")")]] <- as.vector(rbind(
      ifelse(is.na(b), "", paste0(sprintf("%.3f", b), stars)),
      ifelse(is.na(b), "", sprintf("(%.3f)", se))))
  }
  fe_label <- switch(kind, agency="Agency, committee, issue, president FEs",
    nonbureau="Witness type, issue, committee, president FEs", aggregate="Issue, committee, president FEs")
  info <- data.frame(Term = c(if (controls) "Controls", fe_label,
    if (kind != "aggregate") "Witness-hearing FE", if (kind == "nonbureau") "Bureaucrat appeared in hearing",
    "Mean outcome measure", "N", "Adjusted R-squared"))
  for (j in seq_along(models)) {
    m <- models[[j]]
    info[[paste0("(", j, ")")]] <- c(if (controls) "Yes",
      ifelse("witness_id" %in% m$rep_fe, "", "Yes"),
      if (kind != "aggregate") ifelse("witness_id" %in% m$rep_fe, "Yes", ""),
      if (kind == "nonbureau") ifelse(j %in% c(3, 6), "Yes", ""),
      sprintf("%.1f", if (is.null(means)) mean(fitted(m) + resid(m)) else means[j]), format(nobs(m), big.mark = ","),
      sprintf("%.3f", fixest::r2(m, "ar2")))
  }
  bind_rows(out, info)
}
rep_table_v2 <- function(x, caption, label, groups = c(" "=1, Legislative=(ncol(x)-1)/2, Oversight=(ncol(x)-1)/2)) {
  tab <- table_v2(x, caption, label=label) %>% kableExtra::add_header_above(groups, font_size = if (label == "extension-content") 8) %>%
    kableExtra::column_spec(1, width="2.2in")
  boundary <- which(x$Term %in% c("Controls", "Agency, committee, issue, president FEs",
    "Witness type, issue, committee, president FEs", "Issue, committee, president FEs"))[1] - 1L
  tab <- kableExtra::row_spec(tab, boundary, extra_latex_after="\\midrule")
  if (label == "extension-content") {
    tab <- kableExtra::row_spec(tab, 0:nrow(x), font_size = 8)
    tab <- sub("\\begin{tabular}", "\\begingroup\\setlength{\\extrarowheight}{-1pt}\\begin{tabular}", tab, fixed = TRUE)
    tab <- sub("\\end{tabular}", "\\end{tabular}\\endgroup", tab, fixed = TRUE)
  }
  tab
}
rep_note_v2 <- "Standard errors clustered at the hearing level are in parentheses. FE = fixed effect; LES = Legislative Effectiveness Score. * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001, following Ban et al. (2026)."

```

The data come from the [replication archive](https://dataverse.harvard.edu/dataset.xhtml?persistentId=doi:10.7910/DVN/RTYPSG) of @ban2026. The [project repository](https://github.com/jodypark/plsc508_political_networks/tree/main/replication-extension) holds the code and download instructions for the larger files. The main file `dyad_b.dta` pairs each bureaucratic witness with each member who questioned that witness in a House hearing. It covers `r format(n_distinct(dyad_b_raw$hearingid), big.mark = ",")` hearings in the 105th through 113th Congresses (1997--2014). It has `r format(nrow(dyad_b_raw), big.mark = ",")` witness--member rows with `r n_distinct(dyad_b_raw$asker)` members and `r n_distinct(dyad_b_raw$agencycode)` agency codes. Its `r format(n_distinct(dyad_b_raw$witness_id), big.mark = ",")` witness identifiers mark appearances in hearings. The same person can appear under several identifiers.

The outcome is the analytical score (`ascore`) of @ban2026. It measures how much of a witness's answers to one member use falsifiable statements about the policy under discussion. The scale runs from 0 to 100. Observed values range from `r sprintf("%.2f", min(dyad_b_raw$ascore, na.rm = TRUE))` to `r sprintf("%.2f", max(dyad_b_raw$ascore, na.rm = TRUE))`. The score measures analytical content. It does not measure accuracy or influence on policy. The out-partisan indicator $O_{mh}$ follows the replication code. It equals 1 when member $m$ in hearing $h$ does not share the president's party.

For the questioning ties hypothesis (H1), I define member--agency alignment as $C_{ma}=R_m\tilde{I}_a$. Here $R_m$ equals 1 for Republicans and $-1$ for Democrats. The term $\tilde{I}_a$ is the Richardson score of agency $a$ centered at the median agency [@richardson2018]. Higher scores are more conservative. A positive $C_{ma}$ means that the member's party and the agency lean the same way. The measure is an alignment gradient and not a distance on a common scale. For the analytical content hypothesis (H2), I define presidential alignment as $P_{at}=R_{p(t)}\tilde{I}_a$. The term $R_{p(t)}$ codes the party of the president in Congress $t$ in the same way. A positive $P_{at}$ means that the agency leans toward the president's party. Both products measure agency alignment, one with a member and one with the president. I keep the original rows and coding for the replication. I harmonize agency scores only for the extension.

## Hearing Coverage {.unnumbered}

Table \@ref(tab:network-data) reports the observed network in each Congress. Coverage generally grows through the 112th Congress. The 105th Congress has 194 hearings with 134 questioning members. The 110th through 112th Congresses each have more than 1,000 hearings. The 113th Congress has 831 hearings but nearly as many members as the 112th. Density ranges from 0.10 to 0.15 across Congresses and peaks in the 112th. The table counts only members and agencies that appear in the data. Density divides observed ties by the product of observed members and agency codes. Without committee rosters it is not a share of eligible pairs.

## Network Construction {.unnumbered}

For each Congress $t$, I set $y_{ma,t}=1$ when member $m$ questions a witness from agency $a$ at least once. Members form one mode of the network and agency codes form the other. Ties are undirected because a witness's answer does not create a second tie. Edge weights count the witness--member--hearing rows behind each tie. I keep all agency codes in the graph. The Department of Defense code (DD) pools the department with its three military departments. I keep it as one vertex because the replication data assign one code to all four units.

The member projection counts the agencies each pair of members share. It describes shared audiences. It does not record any exchange between members. Analytical content exists only for observed exchanges. A pair without a tie has an undefined content score and not a score of zero.

```{r network-data, eval=TRUE, results='asis'}
# read the original bureaucratic witness dyads
hw_data <- dyad_b_raw
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(hw_data$dyad_id),
          !anyNA(hw_data[c("asker", "agencycode", "congress")]),
          all(nzchar(hw_data$agencycode)))
hw_congress <- focal_congress

# reproduce table 2 appointment and presidential alignment coding
hw_data <- hw_data %>%
  mutate(pas = as.numeric(polappt_type == "PAS"),
         pas = ifelse(agencycode == "DD", NA_real_, pas),
         pas = ifelse(!is.na(dod_pol), dod_pol, pas),
         outparty = 1 - pres_party,
         appointment = case_when(
           pas == 1 ~ "PAS / Defense political",
           polappt == 0 | (agencycode == "DD" & dod_pol == 0) ~ "Career / Defense nonpolitical",
           TRUE ~ "Other / unknown"),
         party = case_when(party_code == 100 ~ "Democrat",
                           party_code == 200 ~ "Republican",
                           TRUE ~ "Other"))
hw_sample <- hw_data %>% filter(congress == hw_congress)

# a tie records participation; weight counts witness-member-hearing rows
hw_edges <- hw_sample %>%
  group_by(asker, agencycode) %>%
  summarise(weight = n(), .groups = "drop")
hw_members <- hw_sample %>% distinct(asker, party)
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(hw_members$asker))
hw_members <- hw_members %>% arrange(asker)
hw_agencies <- sort(unique(hw_sample$agencycode))
hw_B <- matrix(0, nrow(hw_members), length(hw_agencies),
               dimnames = list(paste0("M", hw_members$asker), hw_agencies))
hw_B[cbind(match(hw_edges$asker, hw_members$asker),
           match(hw_edges$agencycode, hw_agencies))] <- hw_edges$weight
hw_g <- graph_from_biadjacency_matrix(hw_B, weighted = TRUE)
hw_binary <- 1L * (hw_B > 0)

# the member projection counts shared agencies, not direct member exchanges
hw_shared <- tcrossprod(hw_binary)
diag(hw_shared) <- 0
hw_project <- graph_from_adjacency_matrix(hw_shared, mode = "undirected",
                                          weighted = TRUE, diag = FALSE)
stopifnot(is_bipartite(hw_g), !is_directed(hw_g),
          ecount(hw_g) == nrow(hw_edges))


network_sample <- hw_sample
edges_v2 <- hw_edges
members_v2 <- hw_members %>% mutate(Node = paste0("M", asker))
agencies_v2 <- data.frame(agencycode = hw_agencies)
B_v2 <- hw_B; binary_v2 <- hw_binary; graph_v2 <- hw_g; project_v2 <- hw_project
coverage_v2 <- dyad_b_raw %>% group_by(congress) %>% summarise(
  Members = n_distinct(asker), Agencies = n_distinct(agencycode),
  Ties = n_distinct(asker, agencycode), Pairs = n(), Hearings = n_distinct(hearingid),
  .groups = "drop") %>% mutate(Density = Ties / (Members * Agencies))
table_v2(coverage_v2, "Observed member--agency networks by Congress", label = "network-data")
```

## Agency Attributes {.unnumbered}

Figure \@ref(fig:vertex-distributions) shows the attributes of unique vertices in the 113th Congress. Each agency and each member counts once. The Richardson score is the primary measure of agency ideology [@richardson2018]. The two Selin scores measure decision-maker and policy-decision independence [@selin2015]. Of all 64 agency codes, 52 have an ideology score and 53 have each Selin score [@selin2015]. I set the ideology and Selin scores of the Department of Defense to missing in the network displays and the extension models. Its military departments do not share one verified parent score. This rule does not change the replication variables.

The dynamic ideal points of @acs2025 vary by administration. Only 11 agency codes have a direct parent-level match to those estimates. I therefore use them only for robustness and join them by the actual administration. I do not average bureau scores into a parent score. Appendix B describes the crosswalk and reports coverage for each attribute.

```{r agency-audit, eval=TRUE, include=FALSE}
# conflicting constituent scores stay missing; never weight by pair frequency
one_score_v2 <- function(x) {
  z <- unique(x[!is.na(x)])
  if (length(z) == 1L) z else NA_real_
}
agency_scores_v2 <- dyad_b_raw %>% group_by(agencycode) %>% summarise(
  across(c(agency_ideo, selin_ind1, selin_ind2), one_score_v2),
  ideology_values = n_distinct(agency_ideo, na.rm = TRUE),
  selin1_values = n_distinct(selin_ind1, na.rm = TRUE),
  selin2_values = n_distinct(selin_ind2, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  # dd pools military departments; partial constituent scores do not identify parent ideology
  mutate(across(c(agency_ideo, selin_ind1, selin_ind2), ~ ifelse(agencycode == "DD", NA_real_, .x)))
agency_audit_v2 <- agency_attributes %>% left_join(agency_scores_v2, by = "agencycode")
# l1_four_level holds the fazekas et al. (2023) agency types, which follow dahlström et al. (2021)
attribute_coverage_v2 <- data.frame(Attribute = c("Richardson", "Selin dimension 1", "Selin dimension 2", "L1 category", "Regulatory source", "Acs direct key"),
  Observed = c(sum(!is.na(agency_audit_v2$agency_ideo)), sum(!is.na(agency_audit_v2$selin_ind1)),
    sum(!is.na(agency_audit_v2$selin_ind2)), sum(!is.na(agency_audit_v2$l1_four_level)),
    sum(!is.na(agency_audit_v2$regulatory)), sum(!is.na(agency_audit_v2$acs_agency_id)))) %>%
  mutate(Total = nrow(agency_audit_v2), Missing = Total - Observed)
regulatory_audit_v2 <- agency_audit_v2 %>%
  mutate(l1_four_level = coalesce(l1_four_level, "Missing"),
    regulatory = ifelse(is.na(regulatory), "Missing", as.character(regulatory))) %>%
  count(l1_four_level, regulatory, .drop = FALSE)
science_support_v2 <- dyad_b_raw %>% left_join(agency_attributes, by = "agencycode") %>%
  count(science_flag, pres_party, oversight, name = "Pairs")
acs_selection_v2 <- dyad_b_raw %>% left_join(agency_attributes %>% select(agencycode, acs_agency_id), by = "agencycode") %>%
  group_by(DirectAcs = !is.na(acs_agency_id)) %>% summarise(Agencies = n_distinct(agencycode), Pairs = n(), .groups = "drop")
```

```{r vertex-distributions, eval=TRUE, fig.cap="Attributes of unique agencies and members in 113th Congress", fig.height=6, fig.note="Each agency and member counts once. Richardson et al. (2018) measure survey-based agency ideology: negative scores are liberal and positive scores conservative. Selin (2015) dimension 1 measures independence of decision makers; dimension 2 measures independence of policy decisions. Missing agency scores are reported explicitly."}
# one observation per focal vertex; missing scores remain explicit
focal_attributes_v2 <- agencies_v2 %>% left_join(agency_audit_v2, by = "agencycode")
vertex_distributions_v2 <- bind_rows(lapply(c("agency_ideo", "selin_ind1", "selin_ind2"), function(v) {
  data.frame(Panel = c(agency_ideo = "(a) Richardson ideology", selin_ind1 = "(b) Selin dimension 1", selin_ind2 = "(c) Selin dimension 2")[[v]],
    Value = focal_attributes_v2[[v]], agencycode = focal_attributes_v2$agencycode)
}))
attribute_panels_v2 <- lapply(unique(vertex_distributions_v2$Panel), function(z) {
  d <- filter(vertex_distributions_v2, Panel == z)
  ggplot(filter(d, !is.na(Value)), aes(Value)) + geom_histogram(bins = 12, fill = pal_v2[1], color = "white") +
    labs(title = z, subtitle = paste("Unique agencies:", nrow(d), "| Missing:", sum(is.na(d$Value))), x = NULL, y = "Agencies") + theme(text = element_text(size = 10))
})
party_panel_v2 <- ggplot(count(members_v2, party), aes(party, n, fill = party)) +
  geom_col() + scale_fill_manual(values = c(Democrat = pal_v2[1], Republican = pal_v2[2], Other = "gray60")) +
  labs(title = "(d) Member party", subtitle = paste("Unique members:", nrow(members_v2), "| Missing:", sum(is.na(members_v2$party))), x = NULL, y = "Members") +
  theme(legend.position = "none", text = element_text(size = 10))
patchwork::wrap_plots(c(attribute_panels_v2, list(party_panel_v2)), ncol = 2)
```

In the 113th Congress, `r sum(!is.na(focal_attributes_v2$agency_ideo))` of the `r nrow(focal_attributes_v2)` agency codes have a Richardson score [@richardson2018]. The median score is $`r sprintf("%.2f", median(focal_attributes_v2$agency_ideo, na.rm = TRUE))`$. Scores range from $`r sprintf("%.2f", min(focal_attributes_v2$agency_ideo, na.rm = TRUE))`$ to `r sprintf("%.2f", max(focal_attributes_v2$agency_ideo, na.rm = TRUE))`. The two Selin dimensions are positively correlated ($r=`r sprintf("%.2f", cor(focal_attributes_v2$selin_ind1, focal_attributes_v2$selin_ind2, use = "complete.obs"))`$) but far from identical [@selin2015]. Ideology and decision-maker independence are only weakly related ($r=`r sprintf("%.2f", cor(focal_attributes_v2$agency_ideo, focal_attributes_v2$selin_ind1, use = "complete.obs"))`$). This weak relation supports treating them as separate moderators. The members are `r sum(members_v2$party == "Democrat")` Democrats and `r sum(members_v2$party == "Republican")` Republicans who questioned at least one agency witness.

# Structure of Congressional Questioning {.unnumbered}

This section describes the questioning network of the 113th Congress in three steps. Centrality shows which agencies reach many members. Closure shows whether members share the same agencies. Community detection shows which groups of members draw on the same set of agencies. Each step says something about how ties form. Each also relates to what members can learn from agency witnesses.

## Agency Reach {.unnumbered}

An agency's reach is the number of distinct members who question its witnesses. In network terms it is the agency's degree. Reach shows how widely an agency's testimony spreads across the House. Figure \@ref(fig:network-plot) draws the bipartite network. Members sit on the left and agencies on the right. Node size shows degree. Agency fill shows the Richardson score [@richardson2018], and gray agencies lack an unambiguous score. Vertical position follows party and degree. It does not encode ideological distance. Figure \@ref(fig:centrality) plots each agency's reach as a share of members against its betweenness.

```{r network-plot, eval=TRUE, fig.cap="Observed questioning network in 113th Congress", fig.height=7, fig.note=paste("Node size shows distinct contacts. Members use party color and shape; agencies use survey-based Richardson et al. (2018) ideology (negative = liberal; positive = conservative). Gray marks agencies without a usable score. The Department of Defense (DD) is gray because it pools four units whose scores differ. Position does not measure ideological distance.", agency_note_v2(names(sort(colSums(binary_v2), decreasing=TRUE))[1:8]))}
# fixed two-mode layout; position is not ideological distance
member_nodes_v2 <- members_v2 %>% mutate(Degree = rowSums(binary_v2)) %>% arrange(party, desc(Degree), asker) %>%
  mutate(x = 0, y = seq(0, 1, length.out = n()))
agency_nodes_v2 <- focal_attributes_v2 %>% mutate(Node = agencycode, Degree = colSums(binary_v2)) %>%
  arrange(desc(Degree), agencycode) %>% mutate(x = 1, y = seq(0, 1, length.out = n()))
network_layout_v2 <- bind_rows(select(member_nodes_v2, Node, x, y), select(agency_nodes_v2, Node, x, y))
network_segments_v2 <- edges_v2 %>% mutate(Node = paste0("M", asker)) %>%
  left_join(select(member_nodes_v2, Node, x, y), by = "Node") %>%
  left_join(select(agency_nodes_v2, agencycode, xend = x, yend = y), by = "agencycode")
# party uses outline/shape; agency ideology uses continuous fill
member_labels_v2 <- member_nodes_v2 %>% group_by(party) %>%
  summarise(y = mean(range(y)), label = paste0(first(party), " (n = ", n(), ")"), .groups = "drop")
network_plot_v2 <- ggplot() + geom_segment(data = network_segments_v2, aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend), color = "gray70", alpha = .13, linewidth = .15) +
  geom_point(data = member_nodes_v2, aes(x, y, color = party, shape = party, size = Degree)) +
  geom_point(data = agency_nodes_v2, aes(x, y, fill = agency_ideo, size = Degree), shape = 22, color = "gray30") +
  geom_text(data = head(agency_nodes_v2, 8), aes(x, y, label = agencycode), nudge_x = .045, hjust = 0, size = 3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Democrat = pal_v2[1], Republican = pal_v2[2], Other = "gray50"), name = "Members") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(Democrat = 16, Republican = 17, Other = 3), name = "Members") +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = pal_v2[1], mid = "white", high = pal_v2[2], midpoint = 0, na.value = "gray65", name = "Agencies: Richardson ideology") +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(.7, 5), guide = "none") +
  annotate("text", x = c(0, 1), y = 1.04, label = c(paste0("Members (n = ", nrow(member_nodes_v2), ")"), paste0("Agencies (n = ", nrow(agency_nodes_v2), ")")), size = 3) +
  geom_text(data = member_labels_v2, aes(x = -.04, y = y, label = label), hjust = 1, size = 3) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-.4, 1.2), clip = "off") + theme_void(base_size = 10) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.box = "vertical", plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA))
network_plot_v2
```

```{r centrality, eval=TRUE, fig.cap="Agency reach and binary betweenness", fig.height=5, fig.note=paste("Degree counts distinct member contacts; degree share divides by observed members. Strength counts witness--member--hearing rows. Normalized binary betweenness is the share of shortest paths through a vertex, with edge weights ignored. Color uses survey-based Richardson et al. (2018) ideology (negative = liberal; positive = conservative). Gray marks agencies without a usable score. The Department of Defense (DD) is gray because it pools four units whose scores differ.", agency_note_v2(c("DD", "HE", "TR", "ST", "HS", "TN")))}
# binary path measures; strength counts pair rows
centrality_v2 <- data.frame(Node = V(graph_v2)$name, Mode = ifelse(V(graph_v2)$type, "Agency", "Member"),
  Degree = degree(graph_v2), DegreeShare = degree(graph_v2) / ifelse(V(graph_v2)$type, nrow(binary_v2), ncol(binary_v2)),
  Strength = strength(graph_v2), Eigenvector = eigen_centrality(graph_v2, weights = NA)$vector,
  Betweenness = betweenness(graph_v2, weights = NA, normalized = TRUE))
agency_centrality_v2 <- centrality_v2 %>% filter(Mode == "Agency") %>% left_join(agency_scores_v2, by = c("Node" = "agencycode"))
centrality_plot_v2 <- ggplot(agency_centrality_v2, aes(DegreeShare, Betweenness)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = Strength, color = agency_ideo), alpha = .8) +
  geom_text(data = filter(agency_centrality_v2, rank(-Degree) <= 5 | Node == "TN"), aes(label = Node), nudge_y = .002, size = 3) +
  scale_color_gradient2(low = pal_v2[1], mid = "gray85", high = pal_v2[2], na.value = "gray60", name = "Richardson ideology") +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(2, 7)) + labs(x = "Share of observed members contacted", y = "Normalized binary betweenness") + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
centrality_plot_v2
```

A few cabinet departments reach many members. The network has `r nrow(binary_v2)` members and `r ncol(binary_v2)` agency codes joined by `r format(sum(binary_v2), big.mark = ",")` ties. These ties rest on `r format(nrow(network_sample), big.mark = ",")` witness--member rows. The median member questioned `r median(rowSums(binary_v2))` agencies and the most active member questioned `r max(rowSums(binary_v2))`. Reach varies much more across agencies. The median agency reached `r median(colSums(binary_v2))` members. The Department of Defense (DD) reached `r colSums(binary_v2)[["DD"]]` members or `r round(100 * colSums(binary_v2)[["DD"]] / nrow(binary_v2))` percent of those observed. The Department of Health and Human Services (HE) follows with `r colSums(binary_v2)[["HE"]]` members and the Department of the Treasury (TR) with `r colSums(binary_v2)[["TR"]]`. The Department of State (ST) with `r colSums(binary_v2)[["ST"]]` members and the Department of Homeland Security (HS) with `r colSums(binary_v2)[["HS"]]` complete the top five. These five departments hold `r round(100 * sum(sort(colSums(binary_v2), decreasing = TRUE)[1:5]) / sum(binary_v2))` percent of all ties. Their reach likely reflects broad jurisdictions. Each runs programs that fall under several House committees. Witnesses from the Department of Defense alone appeared before `r n_distinct(network_sample$committee_name[network_sample$agencycode == "DD"])` of the `r n_distinct(network_sample$committee_name)` committees in the data.

Reach does not follow ideology. Among agencies with a score, the correlation between degree and the Richardson score is $r=`r sprintf("%.3f", cor(agency_centrality_v2$Degree, agency_centrality_v2$agency_ideo, use = "complete.obs"))`$ [@richardson2018]. The agencies with the widest reach are large departments with broad portfolios. Betweenness is the share of shortest paths between other vertices that pass through a given vertex [@borgatti2006]. Most of the agencies with the widest reach also have high betweenness. The Office of the United States Trade Representative (TN) is the main exception. It reached only `r colSums(binary_v2)[["TN"]]` members but ranks fourth in betweenness. Its witnesses appeared before `r n_distinct(network_sample$committee_name[network_sample$agencycode == "TN"])` committees with different jurisdictions. The ties of this office therefore connect members across several committees.

For information sharing, concentrated reach means that a few departments supply a large share of what members hear. The Department of Defense alone accounts for `r round(100 * mean(network_sample$agencycode == "DD"))` percent of witness--member rows. Any average gap across exchanges therefore weighs these departments heavily. A pair-level estimate can reflect the behavior of the Departments of Defense and Health and Human Services more than that of the typical agency.

## Shared Audiences {.unnumbered}

Ordinary triangles cannot form in this network. A tie links a member to an agency and never joins two members or two agencies. The smallest closed cycle therefore has four vertices, in which two members both question the same two agencies. Closure in this setting means that members who question the same agency also share other agencies. Their audiences overlap. I measure closure because overlap would make ties depend on one another. Pair-level models of questioning assume that they do not. I measure it in two ways. Four-cycles count cases in which two members share two agencies. Clustering in the member projection asks whether two members linked to a third member are also linked to each other. Projection inflates this clustering because every agency creates a clique among the members who question it. Table \@ref(tab:closure) compares the observed values with 99 reference networks. Each reference draw keeps every member's number of agencies and assigns agencies at random.

```{r closure, eval=TRUE, results='asis'}
# calculate three nontrivial closure summaries from the incidence matrix
closure_closure <- function(B) {
  shared <- tcrossprod(B)
  common <- shared[upper.tri(shared)]
  diag(shared) <- 0
  g <- graph_from_adjacency_matrix(1L * (shared > 0),
                                   mode = "undirected", diag = FALSE)
  c(Global = transitivity(g, type = "global", isolates = "zero"),
    MeanLocal = transitivity(g, type = "average", isolates = "zero"),
    FourCycles = sum(common * (common - 1) / 2))
}
closure_observed <- closure_closure(binary_v2)
closure_bipartite_triangles <- sum(count_triangles(graph_v2)) / 3
stopifnot(closure_bipartite_triangles == 0)

# randomize agency choices, retaining every member's observed degree
# this reference does not preserve agency degree or committee opportunities
set.seed(508)
closure_draws <- 99
closure_null <- replicate(closure_draws, {
  B <- matrix(0L, nrow(binary_v2), ncol(binary_v2))
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(B))) {
    B[i, sample.int(ncol(B), rowSums(binary_v2)[i])] <- 1L
  }
  closure_closure(B)
})
closure_closure_table <- data.frame(
  Measure = c("Global clustering", "Mean local clustering", "Four-cycles"), Observed = unname(closure_observed),
  NullMean = rowMeans(closure_null),
  NullLow = apply(closure_null, 1, quantile, probs = 0.025),
  NullHigh = apply(closure_null, 1, quantile, probs = 0.975))
closure_v2 <- closure_observed
closure_reference_v2 <- closure_closure_table
table_v2(rename(closure_reference_v2, `Reference mean`=NullMean, `2.5 percentile`=NullLow, `97.5 percentile`=NullHigh), "Closure versus 99 row-degree-preserving reference draws", label = "closure")
```

The observed network has `r format(closure_v2[["FourCycles"]], big.mark = ",")` four-cycles. The reference draws average `r format(round(closure_reference_v2$NullMean[3]), big.mark = ",")`, and their 95 percent interval ends at `r format(round(closure_reference_v2$NullHigh[3]), big.mark = ",")`. Global clustering in the projection is `r sprintf("%.2f", closure_v2[["Global"]])` against `r sprintf("%.2f", closure_reference_v2$NullMean[1])` in the reference. Mean local clustering is `r sprintf("%.2f", closure_v2[["MeanLocal"]])` against `r sprintf("%.2f", closure_reference_v2$NullMean[2])`. Pairs of members thus share two agencies about `r sprintf("%.1f", closure_v2[["FourCycles"]] / closure_reference_v2$NullMean[3])` times as often as members with the same activity would by chance.

The reference has two limits. It does not hold agency degree fixed. Part of the excess could come from the popularity of the Departments of Defense and Health and Human Services alone. It also ignores committee opportunities. Members of one committee meet the same witnesses by design. Closure here may therefore reflect committee structure more than member choice.

For information sharing, closure means that an agency's testimony reaches members who already hear from the same other agencies. These members can compare what several agencies say about related programs. The overlap also shows that ties are not independent. This dependence is one reason to test the questioning ties hypothesis (H1) with a network model.

## Communities and Committees {.unnumbered}

Community detection asks whether members cluster into groups that draw on the same agencies. Two structures could produce such groups. Committees could create them because members of one committee hear the same witnesses. Party could create them if members of each party seek out agencies that share their views. For information sharing, groups that follow committees would hear agency testimony as bipartisan audiences. Groups that follow party would hear it in separate partisan circles.

Figure \@ref(fig:communities) shows Louvain communities in the weighted member projection. Edge weights count shared agencies. Node size counts contacted agencies and shape marks party. Projection can create groups when many members question one popular agency [@lo2026]. I therefore compare the Louvain partition with a Walktrap partition on the same projection [@yang2016].

```{r communities, eval=TRUE, fig.cap="Louvain communities in the weighted shared-agency member projection", fig.height=7, fig.note="Louvain communities use shared-agency counts in the member projection and seed 508. Node size counts agency contacts; shape marks member party. Edges represent shared agencies, not direct communication."}
# use shared-agency counts as similarities for both algorithms
set.seed(508)
hw_louvain <- cluster_louvain(hw_project, weights = E(hw_project)$weight)
hw_walktrap <- cluster_walktrap(hw_project, weights = E(hw_project)$weight,
                                steps = 4)
hw_communities <- list(Louvain = hw_louvain, Walktrap = hw_walktrap)
hw_modularity <- data.frame(
  Algorithm = names(hw_communities),
  Groups = sapply(hw_communities, function(x) length(unique(membership(x)))),
  Modularity = sapply(hw_communities, function(x)
    modularity(hw_project, membership(x), weights = E(hw_project)$weight)))
hw_agreement <- compare(hw_louvain, hw_walktrap, method = "adjusted.rand")

# compare the same partition with party and modal observed committee
hw_modal_committee <- hw_sample %>% count(asker, committee_name) %>%
  arrange(asker, desc(n), committee_name) %>% group_by(asker) %>%
  slice_head(n = 1) %>% ungroup()
hw_member_groups <- hw_members %>%
  mutate(Community = as.integer(membership(hw_louvain)[paste0("M", asker)]),
         Committee = hw_modal_committee$committee_name[
           match(asker, hw_modal_committee$asker)])
hw_party_ari <- compare(hw_member_groups$Community,
                        as.integer(factor(hw_member_groups$party)),
                        method = "adjusted.rand")
hw_committee_ari <- compare(hw_member_groups$Community,
                            as.integer(factor(hw_member_groups$Committee)),
                            method = "adjusted.rand")
hw_composition <- hw_member_groups %>% group_by(Community) %>%
  summarise(Members = n(), Democrats = sum(party == "Democrat"),
            Republicans = sum(party == "Republican"),
            TopCommittee = names(which.max(table(Committee))),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(TopCommittee = sub("^Committee on (the )?", "", TopCommittee))

# identify each community's most frequently contacted agency code
hw_agency_groups <- hw_edges %>%
  left_join(hw_member_groups %>% select(asker, Community), by = "asker") %>%
  group_by(Community, agencycode) %>% summarise(Contacts = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(Community, desc(Contacts), agencycode) %>% group_by(Community) %>%
  slice_head(n = 1) %>% ungroup() %>%
  rename(TopAgency = agencycode)
hw_composition <- left_join(hw_composition, hw_agency_groups, by = "Community")
louvain_v2 <- hw_louvain; walktrap_v2 <- hw_walktrap
member_groups_v2 <- hw_member_groups; community_composition_v2 <- hw_composition
community_agreement_v2 <- data.frame(Comparison = c("Louvain / Walktrap", "Louvain / party", "Louvain / modal committee"),
  ARI = c(hw_agreement, hw_party_ari, hw_committee_ari))
# okabe-ito colors separate communities; shape carries party
set.seed(508)
hw_project_xy <- layout_with_fr(hw_project, weights = E(hw_project)$weight)
hw_group_colors <- pal_v2[c(5, 1, 3, 4, 7, 6, 2)][
                       seq_len(max(hw_member_groups$Community))]
op <- par(mar = c(3, 1, 1, 1), ps = 10)
plot(hw_project, layout = hw_project_xy, vertex.label = NA,
     vertex.size = 3 + sqrt(rowSums(hw_binary)) / 2,
     vertex.color = hw_group_colors[hw_member_groups$Community[match(V(hw_project)$name, paste0("M", hw_member_groups$asker))]],
     vertex.frame.color = NA,
     vertex.shape = ifelse(hw_members$party == "Democrat", "circle", ifelse(hw_members$party == "Republican", "square", "triangle")),
     edge.color = adjustcolor("gray50", alpha.f = 0.04),
     edge.width = 0.15 + log1p(E(hw_project)$weight) / 5)
legend("topleft", paste("Community", seq_along(hw_group_colors)),
       col = hw_group_colors, pch = 16, pt.cex = 1.6, cex = 1, bty = "n")
legend("bottom", c("Democrat", "Republican"), pch = c(16, 15),
       col = "gray30", pt.cex = 1.6, cex = 1, horiz = TRUE,
       bty = "n", inset = c(0, -0.07), xpd = NA)
par(op)
community_plot_v2 <- recordPlot()
```

```{r community-composition, results='asis'}
# describe observed community membership
table_v2(community_composition_v2 %>% rename(Agency = TopAgency, Committee = TopCommittee),
  "Louvain composition with leading agency and modal observed committee", 0, label = "community-composition")
```

Louvain finds `r length(unique(membership(louvain_v2)))` communities with a modularity of `r sprintf("%.2f", hw_modularity$Modularity[1])`. This modularity is low because the projection is dense. In it `r round(100 * edge_density(project_v2))` percent of member pairs share at least one agency. Walktrap finds `r hw_modularity$Groups[2]` groups with a modularity of `r sprintf("%.2f", hw_modularity$Modularity[2])`. Its partition agrees only modestly with Louvain (adjusted Rand index `r sprintf("%.2f", community_agreement_v2$ARI[1])`; Appendix C).

Table \@ref(tab:community-composition) describes each Louvain community. A cabinet department leads each one. The Department of Defense leads the largest community of `r max(community_composition_v2$Members)` members. Its most common committee is Armed Services. The Department of the Treasury leads a community tied to Financial Services. The Department of Energy leads one tied to Energy and Commerce. The Department of Health and Human Services pairs with Oversight and Government Reform. The Department of Homeland Security pairs with the Judiciary Committee. The leading agency counts distinct member ties within the community. The modal committee comes from observed questioning and is not a roster.

Party does not separate the communities. Democrats make up between `r round(100 * min(community_composition_v2$Democrats / community_composition_v2$Members))` and `r round(100 * max(community_composition_v2$Democrats / community_composition_v2$Members))` percent of each community. The adjusted Rand index between communities and party is $`r sprintf("%.3f", community_agreement_v2$ARI[2])`$. The index for modal committee is `r sprintf("%.2f", community_agreement_v2$ARI[3])`. Committee jurisdiction thus appears to drive tie formation more than party does. Members meet agencies through the committees they serve on.

The consequence for information sharing is that an agency's testimony reaches a bipartisan audience defined by jurisdiction. Copartisans and out-partisans of the president sit in the same communities. The partisan gap in @ban2026 arises inside these shared audiences. Members of the two parties do not sort into separate agency groups. Community membership comes from the outcome network. I use it to describe the network and not as a covariate.

# Alignment and Analytical Content {.unnumbered}

This section first reproduces the published estimates. It then reports the extension estimates for the analytical content hypothesis (H2) and the agency independence hypothesis (H3). It closes with the network model for the questioning ties hypothesis (H1).

## Replication Baseline {.unnumbered}

I reproduce Tables 2 through 4 of @ban2026 along with Table B8 of their appendix. I translate their Stata scripts to R and use their data without change. Appendix A reports each table. Every coefficient I checked matches the published value at reported precision. The clustered standard errors and sample sizes match as well. In the first legislative model of Table 2, the out-partisan coefficient is $-1.40$ (SE 0.14).

Table B8 is the closest published test of the analytical content hypothesis (H2). @ban2026 code an agency as liberal when its Richardson score falls below the median of $-0.126$ [@richardson2018]. They place agencies without a score in the nonliberal group. In legislative hearings the interaction between out-partisanship and alignment is $-0.61$ (SE 0.21). In oversight hearings it is $-0.58$ (SE 0.22).

When I instead restrict the sample to agencies with a score, the legislative sample falls from 30,117 to 27,194 rows (Table \@ref(tab:rep-b8-sensitivity)). The legislative interaction stays at $-0.62$ (SE 0.21). The oversight sample falls from 27,401 to 22,545 rows. Its interaction shrinks to $-0.29$ (SE 0.24) and is no longer significant at the 5 percent level. The oversight estimate thus depends on how @ban2026 code agencies without a score. The continuous measure avoids the cutoff but also drops agencies without a score.

## Extension Design and Estimates {.unnumbered}

I estimate a content model that extends the pair-level design of @ban2026. Let $b$ index witnesses and $m$ members. Let $h$ index hearings and $a$ agencies, and let $t$ index Congresses. The content model is

\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
Y_{bmh} = {} & \beta_1 O_{mh} + \beta_2 P_{at} + \beta_3 O_{mh}P_{at}
  + \beta_4 O_{mh}S_{1a} + \beta_5 O_{mh}S_{2a} \\
 & + \boldsymbol{\gamma}^{\top}\mathbf{X}_{bmh}
  + \alpha_a + \alpha_c + \alpha_i + \alpha_p + \varepsilon_{bmh}
\end{aligned}
(\#eq:content)
\end{equation}

where $Y_{bmh}$ is the mean analytical score of the answers that witness $b$ gives member $m$ in hearing $h$. The indicator $O_{mh}$ equals 1 when the member does not share the president's party. The term $P_{at}$ is presidential alignment as defined above. The terms $S_{1a}$ and $S_{2a}$ are the Selin scores for the independence of decision makers and of policy decisions [@selin2015]. I standardize both over unique agencies. The vector $\mathbf{X}_{bmh}$ holds the original controls for the witness and the member along with the hearing and the question. The vector $\boldsymbol{\gamma}$ holds their coefficients. The terms $\alpha_a$ and $\alpha_c$ are agency and committee fixed effects. The terms $\alpha_i$ and $\alpha_p$ are issue and president fixed effects. The term $\varepsilon_{bmh}$ is the error.

Agency fixed effects absorb the main effects of the Selin scores [@selin2015] because the scores do not vary within an agency. Presidential alignment $P_{at}$ changes sign with the president's party, so its main effect stays in the model. The coefficient $\beta_1$ is the out-partisan gap in an agency at the median ideology and the mean of both Selin scores. The coefficient $\beta_3$ is the change in that gap when the agency moves one unit toward the president on the Richardson scale [@richardson2018]. One unit is about the distance between agencies at the 25th and 75th percentiles of that scale. The coefficients $\beta_4$ and $\beta_5$ are the changes in the gap for one standard deviation of each Selin score.

The analytical content hypothesis (H2) predicts $\beta_3<0$. The agency independence hypothesis (H3) predicts $\beta_4>0$ because more independence should shrink a negative gap. I report $\beta_5$ without a directional prediction. For the scientific agencies hypothesis (H4), I add the triple interaction $O_{mh}P_{at}D_a$ with all identified lower-order terms. Here $D_a$ equals 1 for the five science agencies. They are the Department of Energy and the Environmental Protection Agency along with the National Aeronautics and Space Administration. The other two are the National Science Foundation and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission. I estimate legislative and oversight hearings separately as the authors do. Within each hearing type all models use one common sample of pairs with an ideology score and both Selin scores. Standard errors cluster by hearing as in the replication.

```{r extension-content, results='asis'}
# center ideology and standardize independence over unique audited agencies
extension_scores_v2 <- agency_scores_v2 %>% mutate(
  Icenter = agency_ideo - median(agency_ideo, na.rm=TRUE),
  S1 = as.numeric(scale(selin_ind1)), S2 = as.numeric(scale(selin_ind2)))
extension_data_v2 <- rep_b %>% select(-agency_ideo, -selin_ind1, -selin_ind2) %>%
  left_join(extension_scores_v2, by="agencycode") %>%
  left_join(select(agency_attributes, agencycode, science_flag), by="agencycode") %>%
  mutate(P = ifelse(pres %in% c("clinton", "obama"), -1, 1) * Icenter,
    OP = pres_outparty * P, OS1 = pres_outparty * S1, OS2 = pres_outparty * S2,
    OScience = pres_outparty * science_flag, PScience = P * science_flag,
    OPScience = OP * science_flag)
extension_controls_v2 <- c("polappt2", inst_v2[-1], committee_v2, question_v2)
extension_rhs_v2 <- list(
  Alignment=c("pres_outparty", "P", "OP"),
  DecisionMaker=c("pres_outparty", "P", "OP", "OS1"),
  PolicyDecision=c("pres_outparty", "P", "OP", "OS2"),
  Joint=c("pres_outparty", "P", "OP", "OS1", "OS2"),
  Science=c("pres_outparty", "P", "OP", "OS1", "OS2", "OScience", "PScience", "OPScience"))
# use one complete sample within each hearing type for the nested comparisons
extension_complete_v2 <- extension_data_v2 %>% filter(if_all(all_of(c("ascore", "pres_outparty", "P", "OS1", "OS2", "science_flag",
  extension_controls_v2, "agencyid", "presid", "majortopic", "comid", "hid")), ~ !is.na(.x)))
extension_models_v2 <- unlist(lapply(0:1, function(o) lapply(extension_rhs_v2, function(r)
  rep_fit_v2(filter(extension_complete_v2, oversight == o), c(r, extension_controls_v2),
    c("agencyid", "presid", "majortopic", "comid")))), recursive=FALSE)
# display joint and exploratory specifications; separate-moderator fits remain available
extension_main_models_v2 <- extension_models_v2[c(4, 5, 9, 10)]
extension_terms_v2 <- c("pres_outparty", "P", "OP", "OS1", "OS2", "OScience", "PScience", "OPScience")
extension_table_v2 <- rep_display_v2(extension_main_models_v2, extension_terms_v2, controls=TRUE)
table_note_v2(rep_table_v2(extension_table_v2, "Analytical content by continuous agency alignment and independence", "extension-content"),
  paste(rep_note_v2, "The outcome is the analytical score of bureaucratic answers to a member. Columns 1 and 3 include both independence interactions; columns 2 and 4 add the exploratory science interaction and all identified lower-order terms. Agency fixed effects absorb static agency main effects. I center ideology at the median unique agency and standardize each Selin (2015) score over unique agencies. Richardson et al. (2018) provide survey-based ideology: negative is liberal and positive is conservative. Presidential alignment multiplies centered ideology by presidential party (Republican = 1; Democratic = -1). All columns within hearing type use the same complete cases. Estimates describe conditional associations. The exploratory triple interaction is sensitive to omitting the Environmental Protection Agency (Appendix D).",
  "The text defines the five science agencies."))
# retain all estimates and leave-one-science-agency-out sensitivity for appendix d
extension_results_v2 <- bind_rows(lapply(seq_along(extension_models_v2), function(j) {
  m <- extension_models_v2[[j]]
  data.frame(Hearing=ifelse(j <= 5, "Legislative", "Oversight"), Specification=names(extension_rhs_v2)[(j-1)%%5+1],
    Term=names(coef(m)), Estimate=coef(m), SE=fixest::se(m), N=nobs(m))
}))
science_codes_v2 <- c("DN", "EP", "NN", "NF", "NU")
extension_loo_v2 <- bind_rows(lapply(0:1, function(o) bind_rows(lapply(science_codes_v2, function(a) {
  m <- rep_fit_v2(filter(extension_complete_v2, oversight==o, agencycode!=a),
    c(extension_rhs_v2$Science, extension_controls_v2), c("agencyid", "presid", "majortopic", "comid"))
  data.frame(Hearing=ifelse(o==0, "Legislative", "Oversight"), Omitted=a,
    Estimate=unname(coef(m)["OPScience"]), SE=unname(fixest::se(m)["OPScience"]), N=nobs(m))
}))))
```

Table \@ref(tab:extension-content) reports the joint and science models based on Equation \@ref(eq:content). The common samples hold 24,061 legislative and 19,508 oversight pairs. They are smaller than the replication samples of 30,117 and 27,401 pairs because agencies without an ideology score or a Selin score drop out.

In legislative hearings the results support the analytical content hypothesis (H2). At the median agency the out-partisan gap is $-1.20$ (SE 0.19). The interaction between out-partisanship and presidential alignment is $-0.45$ (SE 0.14). In an agency one unit closer to the president the gap is therefore about $-1.65$, which is more than a third larger. Out-partisans lose more of the analysis that copartisans receive when the witness comes from an agency that shares the president's leanings. In oversight hearings the same interaction is $-0.07$ (SE 0.16) and indistinguishable from zero.

The agency independence hypothesis (H3) receives support in oversight hearings only. There the interaction with decision-maker independence is $0.59$ (SE 0.24). At the mean of both Selin scores [@selin2015] the oversight gap is about $-1.00$ (SE 0.25). In an agency one standard deviation more independent the gap is about $-0.42$, which is less than half as large. This pattern fits the account in which the gap reflects the president's control over who leads an agency. In legislative hearings the same interaction is $0.26$ (SE 0.21) and not significant at the 5 percent level. Policy-decision independence shows no clear pattern in the joint models. Its interactions are $-0.16$ (SE 0.21) in legislative and $0.04$ (SE 0.22) in oversight hearings. When I enter each Selin interaction alone [@selin2015], the decision-maker interaction in oversight hearings stays at $0.61$ (SE 0.20; Table \@ref(tab:extension-separate)). The policy-decision interaction rises to $0.35$ (SE 0.19), likely because the two Selin scores are correlated.

The scientific agencies hypothesis (H4) receives little support. In legislative hearings the triple interaction is $-0.33$ (SE 0.41). In oversight hearings it is $-1.00$ (SE 0.50). To check whether one agency drives this estimate, I drop each science agency in turn (Table \@ref(tab:extension-loo)). Without the Environmental Protection Agency the oversight estimate becomes $0.82$ (SE 1.60). Dropping any of the other four agencies leaves it between $-1.16$ and $-0.92$. The oversight result therefore reflects the Environmental Protection Agency and not science agencies as a group.

These estimates describe conditional associations among observed exchanges. Agency ideology and agency independence are not assigned at random. Agencies with independent leaders may also differ in their missions and in the committees that oversee them.

## Network Model {.unnumbered}

For the questioning ties hypothesis (H1), I specify a bipartite exponential random graph model (ERGM) [@cranmer2011; @wang2009]. The model treats the whole network as one outcome. It can therefore account for the dependence among ties that the closure results suggest. The ERGM gives the probability of the observed network in Congress $t$ as

\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(Y_t=y \mid \mathbf{X}_t,\mathcal{R}_t)
=\frac{\exp\{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top} g(y,\mathbf{X}_t)\}}
{\kappa(\boldsymbol{\theta},\mathbf{X}_t,\mathcal{R}_t)}
\end{aligned}
(\#eq:ergm)
\end{equation}

where $Y_t$ is the random member--agency network and $y$ is one possible realization of it. The matrix $\mathbf{X}_t$ holds the member and agency covariates. The set $\mathcal{R}_t$ holds the member--agency pairs with a verified opportunity to meet. The vector $g(y,\mathbf{X}_t)$ holds the network statistics and $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ holds their coefficients. The normalizing constant $\kappa(\boldsymbol{\theta},\mathbf{X}_t,\mathcal{R}_t)$ sums the numerator over all networks allowed by $\mathcal{R}_t$. The statistics are an edge count and a geometrically weighted degree term for each mode. Member party and agency ideology enter as covariates for their modes. Alignment $C_{ma}$ enters as a dyadic covariate. The questioning ties hypothesis (H1) predicts a positive coefficient on $C_{ma}$ in Equation \@ref(eq:ergm). The rival account of @clinton2014 predicts a negative one. I include no triangle term because triangles cannot form in a bipartite network.

The opportunity set is the main data task. Pairs outside it are structural zeros and not observed absences. I will build it in two steps. First, the House committee assignment data of @stewart2017 list the members of each committee in each Congress. Second, the committee of each hearing in the replication data shows which agencies appeared before that committee. A member is eligible to question an agency if the member sat on a committee that heard the agency's witnesses in that Congress. I fit no ERGM until I verify this set.

The 113th Congress remains the main case because it is the most recent Congress in the data and pairs divided government with frequent oversight. I will fit the same specification to each Congress from the 105th to the 113th. A plot of the alignment coefficient by Congress will show whether the result is specific to one Congress. Separate networks for each Congress are common in legislative network research [@fowler2006; @kirkland2014]. Choosing the last Congress of each administration would be a weaker design. The 106th and 110th Congresses had divided government, and so did the 113th. That choice would hold divided government constant and could not separate presidential alignment from House control. As a robustness check, I will fit a temporal ERGM (TERGM) to all nine Congresses with the `btergm` package [@leifeld2018]. Appendix D lists the planned diagnostics. It also describes a comparison of the 111th and 112th Congresses that separates presidential alignment from House control.


```{r ergm, eval=FALSE}
# specification only; verified rosters and structural zeros required before fitting
ergm_congresses <- 105:113
ergm_focal <- 113L
ergm_fits_v2 <- list()
for (congress_id in ergm_congresses) {
  # opportunity_networks_v2 must contain eligible vertices and audited constraints
  net <- opportunity_networks_v2[[as.character(congress_id)]]
  stopifnot(network::get.network.attribute(net, "bipartite") > 0)
  alignment <- alignment_matrices_v2[[as.character(congress_id)]]
  ergm_fits_v2[[as.character(congress_id)]] <- ergm::ergm(
    net ~ edges + gwb1degree(.5, fixed = TRUE) + gwb2degree(.5, fixed = TRUE) +
      b1cov("party") + b2cov("ideology") + edgecov(alignment),
    constraints = opportunity_constraints_v2[[as.character(congress_id)]],
    control = ergm::control.ergm(seed = analysis_seed))
}
# diagnose mcmc and gof before interpreting any coefficient
```

# Discussion {.unnumbered}

The descriptive results and the estimates speak to different stages of information sharing. Committees appear to shape who meets whom. Partisan alignment with the president is associated with what witnesses say once they meet. The extension estimates add that this association varies with agency ideology in legislative hearings and with agency independence in oversight hearings. The questioning ties hypothesis (H1) asks whether agency alignment also shapes the first stage. The answer requires the opportunity set that this draft does not yet have.

## Intergovernmental Context {.unnumbered}

Hearings also bring in witnesses from outside the federal government. Congress often delegates the implementation of federal programs to state governments [@clouser2015; @clouser2016]. Much of this delegation now runs through federal agencies, which shape state roles through waivers and administrative rules [@thompson2013; @metzger2008]. Federal agencies also rely on state and local partners to deliver programs [@clouser2025]. State and local officials can therefore supply information about implementation that federal agencies hold only in part. When state or local officials also testify, members can compare a federal witness's answers with those of officials who run the program. Figure \@ref(fig:hearing-context) shows how often this occurs. It counts unique hearings in the matched sample and marks hearings with at least one state or local government witness.

```{r hearing-context, eval=TRUE, fig.cap="State and local witnesses in hearings across Congresses 105--113th", fig.height=6.5, fig.note="Each hearing counts once. Presence means at least one state or local government witness; co-attendance does not establish cooperation. Labels report the percentage of hearings with such a witness."}
# deduplicate hearings before counting; co-attendance is not cooperation
hearing_context_v2 <- dyad_b_raw %>% group_by(hearingid) %>% summarise(
  congress = first(congress), committee_name = first(committee_name),
  StateLocal = any(n_statelocgov > 0, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
hearing_by_congress_v2 <- hearing_context_v2 %>% count(congress, StateLocal) %>% group_by(congress) %>%
  mutate(Share = n / sum(n)) %>% ungroup()
hearing_by_committee_v2 <- hearing_context_v2 %>% count(committee_name, StateLocal) %>% group_by(committee_name) %>%
  mutate(Total = sum(n), Share = n / Total) %>% ungroup() %>%
  filter(committee_name %in% (hearing_context_v2 %>% count(committee_name, sort = TRUE) %>% slice_head(n = 10) %>% pull(committee_name)))
context_colors_v2 <- c("FALSE" = "gray75", "TRUE" = pal_v2[1])
context_a_v2 <- ggplot(hearing_by_congress_v2, aes(factor(congress), n, fill = StateLocal)) + geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = context_colors_v2, labels = c("Absent", "Present"), name = "State/local witness") +
  geom_text(data = filter(hearing_by_congress_v2, StateLocal), aes(label = paste0(round(100 * Share), "%")), position = position_stack(vjust = .5), size = 2.7, angle = 90) +
  labs(title = "(a) Hearings by Congress", subtitle = "Labels: share with state/local witnesses", x = "Congress", y = "Unique hearings")
context_b_v2 <- ggplot(hearing_by_committee_v2, aes(reorder(sub("^Committee on (the )?", "", committee_name), Total), n, fill = StateLocal)) +
  geom_col() + coord_flip() + scale_fill_manual(values = context_colors_v2, labels = c("Absent", "Present"), name = "State/local witness") +
  labs(title = "(b) Leading parent committees", x = NULL, y = "Unique hearings")
context_a_v2 + context_b_v2 + patchwork::plot_layout(widths = c(1, 1.4), guides = "collect") &
  theme(text = element_text(size = 10), legend.position = "bottom")
```

Of the `r format(nrow(hearing_context_v2), big.mark = ",")` hearings, `r round(100 * mean(hearing_context_v2$StateLocal))` percent include a state or local witness. The share falls from `r with(filter(hearing_by_congress_v2, StateLocal, congress == 105), round(100 * Share))` percent in the 105th Congress to `r with(filter(hearing_by_congress_v2, StateLocal, congress == 113), round(100 * Share))` percent in the 113th. Committees differ as well, probably because their jurisdictions rely on state implementation to different degrees. In the Resources Committee `r with(filter(hearing_by_committee_v2, StateLocal, committee_name == "Committee on Resources"), round(100 * Share))` percent of hearings include a state or local witness. The share is `r with(filter(hearing_by_committee_v2, StateLocal, committee_name == "Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure"), round(100 * Share))` percent in Transportation and Infrastructure. Armed Services hearings almost never include one (`r with(filter(hearing_by_committee_v2, StateLocal, committee_name == "Committee on Armed Services"), round(100 * Share))` percent).

```{r state-local-gap, fig.cap="Conditional out-partisan gap by state/local witness presence", fig.height=4.5, fig.note="Points show the out-partisan minus copartisan analytical-score contrast; bars show 95 percent hearing-clustered t intervals. Separate legislative and oversight models interact presidential out-partisanship with the presence of any state or local witness. They include all original member and hearing controls along with question controls. They also include agency and committee fixed effects along with issue and president fixed effects. State/local presence is measured once per hearing. These are conditional associations among observed exchanges; co-attendance is not cooperation."}
# estimate hearing-context differences in the pair-level analytical score
context_data_v2 <- rep_b %>% left_join(select(hearing_context_v2, hearingid, StateLocal), by="hearingid") %>%
  mutate(StateLocal=as.integer(StateLocal), OStateLocal=pres_outparty * StateLocal)
context_models_v2 <- lapply(0:1, function(o) rep_fit_v2(filter(context_data_v2, oversight==o),
  c("pres_outparty", "StateLocal", "OStateLocal", extension_controls_v2), c("agencyid", "presid", "majortopic", "comid")))
context_gaps_v2 <- bind_rows(lapply(1:2, function(j) {
  m <- context_models_v2[[j]]; b <- coef(m); V <- vcov(m)
  bind_rows(lapply(0:1, function(z) {
    L <- setNames(rep(0, length(b)), names(b)); L["pres_outparty"] <- 1; L["OStateLocal"] <- z
    estimate <- sum(L*b); se <- sqrt(as.numeric(t(L) %*% V %*% L))
    critical <- qt(.975, df=fixest::degrees_freedom(m, "t"))
    data.frame(Hearing=c("Legislative", "Oversight")[j], Presence=c("Absent", "Present")[z+1],
      Estimate=estimate, SE=se, Lower=estimate-critical*se, Upper=estimate+critical*se, N=nobs(m))
  }))
}))
ggplot(context_gaps_v2, aes(Presence, Estimate, color=Hearing)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept=0, linetype=2, color="gray60") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin=Lower, ymax=Upper), position=position_dodge(width=.35)) +
  scale_color_manual(values=pal_v2[1:2]) + labs(x="State/local witness in hearing", y="Out-partisan minus copartisan analytical score", color="Hearing type") +
  theme(legend.position="bottom")
```

Figure \@ref(fig:state-local-gap) asks whether the out-partisan gap differs in hearings with a state or local witness. Each point is the out-partisan minus copartisan contrast from a model that adds the presence indicator and its interaction with out-partisanship. In legislative hearings the gap is nearly the same with and without such a witness ($-1.30$ and $-1.27$). The interaction is $-0.03$ (SE 0.28). In oversight hearings the gap is $-1.56$ (SE 0.13) without a state or local witness and $-0.77$ (SE 0.34) with one. The difference of $0.79$ (SE 0.36) is significant at the 5 percent level. Out-partisans thus receive relatively more analytical content in oversight hearings that include state or local officials. One reading is that federal witnesses answer more fully when officials who run the program can contest their claims. Another is that committees invite state and local witnesses to hearings on less partisan topics. These models use the full replication samples and describe conditional associations.

Co-attendance is not cooperation. The figures show only who testified in the same hearing. They do not show whether state and local officials changed what federal witnesses said.

## Identification and Limits {.unnumbered}

This study has four limits. First, observed questioning does not reveal who sought an invitation or who declined one. It also says nothing about whether members used the information. Second, the network has no opportunity set yet. Density and the closure reference use observed members and agencies only. Third, the extension models estimate conditional associations. Agency ideology and agency independence are not assigned at random. The common samples also drop about a fifth of legislative pairs and nearly three in ten oversight pairs. A network model accounts for dependence among ties but does not identify a causal effect of alignment. I also derive community membership from the outcome network.

Fourth, the institutional measures are static. The Richardson score comes from a 2014 survey [@richardson2018]. The Selin scores come from the statutes in force in 2013 [@selin2015]. Many agencies changed between 1997 and 2014. The Acs estimates vary by administration but cover only 11 agency codes [@acs2025]. Ideology is missing for 12 of 64 agency codes. The Table B8 sensitivity shows that this missingness could change a published result.

# Conclusion {.unnumbered}

I ask whether agency alignment shapes which members question which agencies and what they learn. The House questioning network of the 113th Congress appears to follow committee jurisdiction in part (adjusted Rand index `r sprintf("%.2f", community_agreement_v2$ARI[3])`). A few cabinet departments reach many members. Pairs of members share two agencies about three and a half times as often as a random reference predicts. Communities of members partly follow committees and mix the two parties. The partisan gaps that @ban2026 find therefore arise inside bipartisan audiences that committees assemble.

My replication matches the four published tables at their reported precision. The Table B8 result holds in legislative hearings when I drop agencies without an ideology score. In oversight hearings it falls from $-0.58$ to $-0.29$ and is no longer significant at the 5 percent level. The continuous measures show where the gap varies. In legislative hearings the out-partisan gap widens by about 0.45 points for each unit the agency moves toward the president on the Richardson scale [@richardson2018]. In oversight hearings it narrows by about 0.59 points for each standard deviation of decision-maker independence [@selin2015]. It is also about half as large in oversight hearings with a state or local witness. The science-agency pattern rests on the Environmental Protection Agency.

These results broaden @ban2026 in three ways. First, the network view shows who meets whom before any testimony begins. Second, a continuous measure of agency ideology replaces the median split and shows that the gap varies across the full range of agencies. Third, agency independence links a witness to the president through the agency's structure and not its views. The gap may thus reflect the policy views of agencies in legislative hearings and the president's hold on their leaders in oversight hearings.

Future work can extend these results in four ways. The bipartite ERGM can test whether aligned members question an agency more often once committee rosters define the opportunity set [@stewart2017]. A comparison of the 111th and 112th Congresses can separate presidential alignment from House control because the House majority flipped under the same president. The dynamic estimates of @acs2025 can show whether the gap moves as agencies shift across administrations once they cover more agency codes. Studies of state and local witnesses can test whether officials who run programs change what federal witnesses tell members.

# Appendix A: Replication {.unnumbered}

\setcounter{table}{0}\setcounter{figure}{0}
\renewcommand{\thetable}{A.\arabic{table}}\renewcommand{\theHtable}{A.\arabic{table}}
\renewcommand{\thefigure}{A.\arabic{figure}}\renewcommand{\theHfigure}{A.\arabic{figure}}

This appendix reproduces the four published results I use. I translate the four Stata scripts of @ban2026 to R with `fixest`. The scripts are `TABLE 2.do` and `TABLE A8.do` along with `TABLE 3.do` and `TABLE 4.do`. The translation keeps the one absorbed fixed effect of Stata's `areg` and enters the others as explicit factors. It retains singleton observations. Finite-sample corrections count the absorbed fixed effects as `areg` does. Standard errors cluster by hearing except in Table 4, which clusters by committee. Every coefficient I checked matches the published tables at reported precision. The standard errors and sample sizes also match, as do the adjusted $R^2$ values. Tables report coefficients with clustered standard errors in parentheses. They omit absorbed terms.

## A.1 Table 2 {.unnumbered}

Table \@ref(tab:rep-table2) reproduces Table 2 for bureaucratic witnesses. Columns 1--3 use legislative hearings and columns 4--6 use oversight hearings. Columns 3 and 6 replace agency and committee fixed effects with witness-hearing fixed effects. The appointment indicator follows the script. It codes presidential appointees who require Senate confirmation (PAS) as 1. It sets the Department of Defense to missing before applying the Defense appointee indicator (`dod_pol`). The script also logs question word count.

```{r rep-table2, eval=TRUE, results='asis'}

    rep_fit_v2(d, c(r, question_v2), c("agencyid", "presid", "majortopic", "comid")),
    rep_fit_v2(d, c(r, question_v2), c("witness_id", "presid", "majortopic")))
}), recursive = FALSE)
rep_table2_table <- rep_display_v2(rep_table2_models)

```
