# Appendix B: Data Construction and Measurement {.unnumbered}

\setcounter{table}{0}\setcounter{figure}{0}
\renewcommand{\thetable}{B.\arabic{table}}\renewcommand{\theHtable}{B.\arabic{table}}
\renewcommand{\thefigure}{B.\arabic{figure}}\renewcommand{\theHfigure}{B.\arabic{figure}}

I measure agency attributes at the level of the agency code in @ban2026. The file \fname{additional-data/clean/agency_attributes.csv} has one row for each of the 64 codes. One script builds it from local raw files (\fname{additional-data/clean/clean_agency_attributes.R}). The replication data name each agency with its name in the records of the Office of Personnel Management (OPM). The script standardizes these names and matches them to agency names in the federal contract data of @fazekas2023. It requires an exact match after standardization and uses no fuzzy matching. It does not average scores across bureaus or weight them by pair rows. Missing or conflicting source values stay missing. The replication files of @ban2026 are unchanged.

Table \@ref(tab:agency-audit) reports coverage for all 64 codes. The Richardson score covers 52 codes after the Defense rule [@richardson2018]. Each Selin dimension covers 53 [@selin2015]. The four-level leadership category comes from the agency types in the federal contract data of @fazekas2023. Following @dahlstrom2021, they order these types from most to least exposed to political control. The first two types are executive departments and distinct bureaus within those departments. The third covers independent administrations, which resemble departments in structure but sit outside the cabinet. The fourth covers independent commissions and independent regulatory commissions (IRCs). Members of commission boards often serve fixed terms with protection from removal [@selin2015]. The category covers 33 codes. It is not a binning of the Selin scores [@selin2015]. The file also keeps a binary rule that codes commissions as 1 and cabinet departments as 0. I do not use that rule here.

The regulatory indicator covers 39 codes. It equals 1 when an agency name matches the name of an agency that issues federal rules. The coding first uses exact matches to agencies in the Acs data [@acs2025]. It then matches agencies that issued final rules in the *Federal Register* from 2004 to 2015 and uses fuzzy name matches for the rest. A few fuzzy matches may pair different agencies. I have not audited these matches, so I use the indicator only for description. It records a function and not statutory authority. Table \@ref(tab:regulatory-audit) crosses it with the leadership category. I code no service indicator. An agency without the regulatory flag is not necessarily a service agency. A later audit will code rulemaking and adjudication from the *Sourcebook of United States Executive Agencies*, which lists agencies with statutory adjudicatory authority and their rulemaking activity [@selin2018].

Eleven codes have a direct parent-level match to the Acs estimates [@acs2025]. Table \@ref(tab:acs-selection) shows their share of pair rows. I must join the estimates by the actual administration and not by Congress alone. Cells without an agency--administration estimate stay missing. Some codes pool unusual units. The code for the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NN) includes the Columbia Accident Investigation Board, for example.

The Department of Defense code (DD) pools four OPM units. Their categories and scores do not agree. I leave these values missing and do not choose one unit. All attributes are static. I have not verified that each category applies to every hearing year from 1997 to 2014. Table \@ref(tab:science-support) counts pair rows by the science flag along with presidential copartisanship and hearing type. It shows the support available for the scientific agencies hypothesis (H4).

```{r agency-audit-display, results='asis'}
# report unique-agency coverage and source coding limits
table_v2(attribute_coverage_v2, "Agency attribute coverage: all observed agency codes", 0, label = "agency-audit")
table_v2(rename(regulatory_audit_v2, `Leadership category`=l1_four_level, Regulatory=regulatory, Agencies=n), "Leadership category and regulatory coding (unaudited)", 0, label = "regulatory-audit")
table_v2(acs_selection_v2, "Direct Acs parent-key coverage in pair rows", 0, label = "acs-selection")
table_v2(rename(science_support_v2, `Science agency`=science_flag, `Presidential copartisan`=pres_party, Oversight=oversight), "Exploratory science support by presidential copartisanship and hearing type", 0, label = "science-support")
```

# Appendix C: Additional Network Descriptions {.unnumbered}

\setcounter{table}{0}\setcounter{figure}{0}
\renewcommand{\thetable}{C.\arabic{table}}\renewcommand{\theHtable}{C.\arabic{table}}
\renewcommand{\thefigure}{C.\arabic{figure}}\renewcommand{\theHfigure}{C.\arabic{figure}}

Table \@ref(tab:closure-congress) repeats the closure measures for each Congress. Coverage varies across Congresses, so the comparison is descriptive. Table \@ref(tab:community-algorithms) reports modularity for the Louvain and Walktrap partitions of the same projection. Table \@ref(tab:community-agreement) compares the Louvain partition with the Walktrap partition and with party and modal committee.

```{r closure-congress, results='asis'}
# coverage varies across congresses; this is a descriptive comparison
closure_congress_v2 <- bind_rows(lapply(sort(unique(dyad_b_raw$congress)), function(t) {
  d <- dyad_b_raw %>% filter(congress == t) %>% distinct(asker, agencycode)
  B <- 1L * (table(d$asker, d$agencycode) > 0)
  z <- closure_closure(B)
  data.frame(Congress = t, Members = nrow(B), Agencies = ncol(B),
    Global = z[1], MeanLocal = z[2], FourCycles = z[3])
}))
table_v2(closure_congress_v2, "Closure across observed Congress networks", label = "closure-congress")
table_v2(hw_modularity, "Community algorithms on the identical weighted member projection", label = "community-algorithms")
table_v2(community_agreement_v2, "Louvain agreement with alternative partition and member attributes", label = "community-agreement")
```

Figure \@ref(fig:title-buckets) classifies hearing titles with the seven verb categories developed by Professor Clouser McCann (working paper). The categories describe which government does what under intergovernmental delegation [@clousermccann2026]. I keep the verb lists unchanged and apply them to hearing titles. Titles are short and often lack a verb. I match each listed word as a literal whole word or phrase in the lowercase title. I do not lemmatize titles or identify grammatical subjects. Thus "regulate" matches the regulatory category but "regulation" does not. A title can match several categories. Where a figure needs one category per title, the first match wins. The order runs from enforcement through regulatory and funding to oversight. Consultation and programmatic follow, and operations comes last. Titles with no listed word fall into Other.

Each panel uses the leading agency of one Louvain community from Table \@ref(tab:community-composition). A hearing joins a panel if a witness from that agency appeared. Panels draw on all nine Congresses. A hearing counts once in each panel but can appear in several panels.

```{r title-buckets, eval=TRUE, fig.cap="Hearing title categories by community leading agency", fig.height=6, fig.note=paste("Categories come from the seven verb categories developed by Professor Clouser McCann (working paper). Categories describe literal hearing-title words: enforcement = sanctions and compliance; regulatory = permissions and rules; funding = fiscal transfers; oversight = monitoring and evaluation; consultation = coordination and exchange; programmatic = services and information; operations = administration and implementation. Other means no dictionary match. First-match order follows the listed categories; no lemmatization or testimony coding is used. Panels overlap.", agency_note_v2(community_composition_v2$TopAgency))}
# hearing title wording; literal dictionary phrases, first match in lab precedence
# no lemmatization or testimony coding; unmatched and multiple matches reported below
profile_verbs <- list(
  Enforcement = 'enforce, penalize, prosecute, prohibit, fine, suspend, sanction, terminate, deport, arrest, compel, levy, comply, order, withhold, adjudicate, bar',
  Regulatory = 'approve, certify, license, prescribe, issue, designate, specify, deny, revoke, promulgate, regulate, classify, authorize, permit, waive, amend, modify, repeal, rescind, adopt, reject, exempt, limit, restrict, impose, propose, control, draft, formulate, allow, set, enact, mandate, preempt, recognize, abolish, accredit',
  Funding = 'pay, grant, allocate, appropriate, fund, award, receive, reimburse, distribute, compensate, transfer, expend, apportion, disburse, obligate, obtain, allot, reallot, guarantee, insure',
  Oversight = 'monitor, audit, evaluate, review, investigate, ensure, determine, assess, verify, inspect, examine, oversee, observe, supervise, study, analyze, attest, require, condition',
  Consultation = 'consult, confer, coordinate, cooperate, collaborate, consider, negotiate, meet, engage, partner, agree, encourage, seek, request, facilitate, participate, share, exchange, convene, assemble',
  Programmatic = 'provide, report, submit, notify, develop, serve, publish, disclose, inform, describe, identify, prepare, collect, gather, compile, disseminate, transmit, communicate, train, educate, promote, support, assist, advise, recommend, create, design, define, instruct, furnish, file, pilot, test, demonstrate, guide',
  Operations = 'administer, manage, operate, maintain, conduct, establish, apply, carry out, implement, perform, execute, enter into, use, make, direct, delegate, assign, undertake, contract, run, revise, accept, appoint, exercise, retain, plan, expand, decide, vest, entrust, acquire, construct, procure, convey, hire, employ, devolve') 

profile_verbs <- lapply(profile_verbs, function(x) strsplit(x, ", ", fixed = TRUE)[[1]])
title_hearings_v2 <- dyad_b_raw %>% filter(!is.na(title), nzchar(trimws(title))) %>% distinct(hearingid, title)
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(title_hearings_v2$hearingid))
title_match_v2 <- vapply(profile_verbs, function(words) {
  pattern <- paste0("\\b(", paste(words, collapse = "|"), ")\\b")
  grepl(pattern, tolower(title_hearings_v2$title), perl = TRUE)
}, logical(nrow(title_hearings_v2)))
title_hearings_v2$Matches <- rowSums(title_match_v2)
title_hearings_v2$Bucket <- ifelse(title_hearings_v2$Matches == 0, "Other",
  colnames(title_match_v2)[max.col(title_match_v2, ties.method = "first")])
title_quality_v2 <- data.frame(TitledHearings = nrow(title_hearings_v2),
  MissingTitleHearings = n_distinct(dyad_b_raw$hearingid) - nrow(title_hearings_v2),
  UnmatchedShare = mean(title_hearings_v2$Matches == 0), MultiLabelShare = mean(title_hearings_v2$Matches > 1))
# panel membership uses leading agency; a hearing can appear in several panels
title_panels_v2 <- dyad_b_raw %>% distinct(hearingid, agencycode) %>%
  inner_join(select(community_composition_v2, Community, agencycode = TopAgency), by = "agencycode") %>%
  inner_join(title_hearings_v2, by = "hearingid") %>% distinct(Community, agencycode, hearingid, .keep_all = TRUE)
title_panel_quality_v2 <- title_panels_v2 %>% group_by(Community, agencycode) %>%
  summarise(TitledHearings = n(), UnmatchedShare = mean(Matches == 0),
    MultiLabelShare = mean(Matches > 1), .groups = "drop")
title_buckets_v2 <- title_panels_v2 %>% mutate(agencycode = factor(agencycode, levels = community_composition_v2$TopAgency),
  Bucket = factor(Bucket, levels = rev(c(names(profile_verbs), "Other")))) %>% count(Community, agencycode, Bucket) %>% group_by(Community, agencycode) %>%
  mutate(Share = n / sum(n)) %>% ungroup()
title_plot_v2 <- ggplot(title_buckets_v2, aes(Share, Bucket, fill = Bucket)) + geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~ agencycode, ncol = 3, drop = FALSE) + scale_x_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(round(100*x), "%")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = setNames(c(pal_v2, "gray75"), c(names(profile_verbs), "Other"))) +
  labs(x = "Share of titled hearings (first dictionary match)", y = NULL) +
  theme(text = element_text(size = 10), legend.position = "none")
title_plot_v2
```

```{r title-quality, results='asis'}
# report unmatched and ambiguous title classifications
table_v2(title_quality_v2, "Title dictionary coverage and ambiguity", label = "title-quality")
table_v2(rename(title_panel_quality_v2, Agency=agencycode), "Title dictionary coverage by community leading agency", label = "title-panel-quality")
```

Most titles match no category. Of the `r format(title_quality_v2$TitledHearings, big.mark = ",")` hearings with a title, `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * title_quality_v2$UnmatchedShare)` percent fall into Other. Another `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * title_quality_v2$MultiLabelShare)` percent match more than one category. Tables \@ref(tab:title-quality) and \@ref(tab:title-panel-quality) report these shares. The data also include `r title_quality_v2$MissingTitleHearings` hearings without a title. The measure describes the wording of hearing titles. It says nothing about what witnesses said or what agencies are authorized to do. Any substantive claim needs a validation sample of titles.

# Appendix D: Inferential Diagnostics {.unnumbered}

\setcounter{table}{0}\setcounter{figure}{0}
\renewcommand{\thetable}{D.\arabic{table}}\renewcommand{\theHtable}{D.\arabic{table}}
\renewcommand{\thefigure}{D.\arabic{figure}}\renewcommand{\theHfigure}{D.\arabic{figure}}

This appendix reports checks on the content models. It also lists the planned network diagnostics and robustness designs, since the ERGM remains unfitted.

For the ERGM, I will first verify the opportunity set. Each observed tie must fall inside it, and eligible members without ties stay in the network as isolates. I will then inspect Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) diagnostics for each fit. Goodness of fit compares simulated networks with the observed degree distributions and four-cycles. A coefficient plot will show the alignment estimate with its interval for each Congress from the 105th to the 113th. The TERGM in `btergm` will pool the nine Congresses as a robustness check [@leifeld2018]. Its bootstrapped pseudolikelihood intervals need care in interpretation.

A second planned robustness design compares the 111th Congress (2009--2010) with the 112th (2011--2012). Both served under President Obama, so the president and the agencies stay the same. The House majority switched from Democrats to Republicans after the 2010 election. Each agency's alignment with the president therefore stays fixed while its alignment with the majority party reverses. A change in the alignment coefficient between the two Congresses would point to House control rather than the president. The two networks are also similar in size. They have 422 and 421 members with 1,076 and 1,091 hearings. The Departments of Defense, the Treasury and Health and Human Services reach the most members in both.

For the content models, Table \@ref(tab:extension-separate) enters alignment and each Selin interaction separately [@selin2015]. All columns within a hearing type use the same rows as Table \@ref(tab:extension-content). Differences across columns therefore do not reflect changes in the sample. Relative to the replication samples, the common samples lose 6,056 legislative and 7,893 oversight pairs because the Richardson score [@richardson2018] or a Selin score [@selin2015] is missing. Table \@ref(tab:science-support) reports support in each cell of the science flag and copartisanship by hearing type. Table \@ref(tab:extension-loo) drops each science agency in turn to check whether one agency drives the triple interaction. Dropping the Environmental Protection Agency reverses the sign of the oversight estimate and more than triples its standard error. Dropping any other science agency leaves the estimate between $-1.16$ and $-0.92$.


```{r extension-sensitivity, results='asis'}
# separate moderators on the same complete sample as table 4
table_note_v2(rep_table_v2(rep_display_v2(extension_models_v2[c(1,2,3,6,7,8)],
  c("pres_outparty", "P", "OP", "OS1", "OS2"), controls=TRUE),
  "Alignment and separate independence interactions on common samples", "extension-separate"),
  paste(rep_note_v2, "Columns 1 and 4 include alignment only; columns 2 and 5 add decision-maker independence; columns 3 and 6 add policy-decision independence. Samples and controls match Table \\ref{tab:extension-content}, and so does the scaling."))
table_note_v2(table_v2(extension_loo_v2, "Leave-one-science-agency-out sensitivity of the triple interaction", label="extension-loo"),
  paste("Each row re-estimates the exploratory specification after omitting the named science agency. Estimate and SE (standard error) refer to out-partisanship x continuous presidential alignment x science status. Standard errors cluster by hearing. Omitting the Environmental Protection Agency changes the oversight triple interaction from negative to positive and increases its standard error. These are descriptive conditional associations.", agency_note_v2(science_codes_v2)))
```


# Appendix E: Reproducibility and AI Assistance {.unnumbered}

\setcounter{table}{0}\setcounter{figure}{0}
\renewcommand{\thetable}{E.\arabic{table}}\renewcommand{\theHtable}{E.\arabic{table}}
\renewcommand{\thefigure}{E.\arabic{figure}}\renewcommand{\theHfigure}{E.\arabic{figure}}

The R Markdown file runs from the project directory with the replication data in `bureaucrats_jop/`. It downloads nothing when it knits. Seed 508 fixes the Louvain partition and the network layout along with the closure reference draws. The community results depend on igraph 2.3.3. I tested the replication with fixest 0.14.2. [My GitHub repository for this project](https://github.com/jodypark/plsc508_political_networks/tree/main/replication-extension) holds the code and the additional agency data.

I orchestrated the following tasks in one multi-agent environment using different AI models for research support and coding. I also used them for grammar checks and rubric-based evaluation. 

- Codex GPT-6-Astra set up the document layout and the analysis contracts and built the agency crosswalk from my sample code. It also reviewed the code against the original Stata scripts.
- Codex GPT-6.1-Sol wrote and tested the R chunks for the network displays and the replication tables based on my analysis design.
- Claude Opus 5.5 reviewed the numbers in each interpretation against the code output. It also proofread my writing and checked the \LaTeX output.

I directed each task and checked the final outputs against the underlying sources.
